title: Autoimmunity-associated DIORA1 binds the MRCK family of serine/threonine kinases and controls cell motility
projectDescription: Genetic association links DIORA1 to numerous autoimmune rheumatic diseases including systemic lupus erythematous, Sjögren's disease, myositis, scleroderma and rheumatoid arthritis, but its cellular function remains unknown. Here, we identify the MRCK kinase family as DIORA1 interactors. MRCK kinases regulate the activity of actin-myosin networks, including cell adhesion, motility and invasion. Mapping the interaction between DIORA1 and MRCKs, we found that DIORA1 binds three distinct modules of MRCK kinases, including the conserved autoinhibitory kinase inhibitory motif (KIM) and C1-PH-CNH domains. Knockdown of DIORA1 altered cellular phosphorylation patterns, including reduced phosphorylation of known MRCK targets. Functional analyses revealed enhanced cellular migration and invasion following knockdown of DIORA1, and RNA-sequencing and proteomic analyses confirmed upregulation of epithelial mesenchymal transition genes and proteins. In summary, our findings identify autoimmunity-associated DIORA1 as a previously uncharacterized interactor of MRCK kinases and a modulator of cell motility.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Approximately 40 million SK-N-SH cells per sample were collected (four replicates per condition, i.e., DIORA1 knockdown and non-targeting control for comprehensive phosphoproteomic and total proteomic investigations. Each sample was then partitioned, assigning approximately 20% for total proteomic analysis and 80% for phosphoproteomic analysis. The cell pellets composed of 80% of the collected cells and intended for phosphoproteomic analysis were solubilized in a solution of 6M guanidine hydrochloride, 5 mM Tris(2-carboxyethyl) phosphine , 10 mM chloroacetamide, 100 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.5. The solution was supplemented with a 100x protease inhibitor cocktail (Roche) and sonicated in a water bath using a VibraCell probe (Sonics & Materials, Inc.). After sonication, samples were vortexed and clarified through centrifugation. The protein concentration of each sample was determined using the BCA assay (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and 3 mg of protein per sample was then digested with trypsin (Promega). The samples were vortexed, centrifuged and the resultant peptide mixture was concentrated and purified using a reversed‑phase C18 HyperSep plate (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Peptides were eluted from the plate with a stepwise elution protocol, starting with 30% acetonitrile (ACN)/ 0.1% formic acid (FA), and then followed by 80% ACN/0.1% FA. Samples were dried by vacuum centrifugation (Eppendorf). Phosphopeptides were enriched using a Pierce High-Select Fe-NTA kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. 10 µg aliquots of obtained phosphopeptides were labelled with TMTpro (Thermo Fisher Scientific) by adding TMTpro reagent in ACN, followed by 2 h incubation at room temperature (RT). The reaction was quenched by adding 5% hydroxylamine and incubating for 15 min at RT. All samples were then combined in one vial, fractioned (see below) and an aliquot was subjected to LC-MS/MS analysis. Cell pellets comprising 20% of the previously collected cells and intended for total proteomic investigations were solubilized using an 8M urea solution with 0.2% ProteaseMAX (Promega) and 5% ACN in 100 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0, further supplemented with a 100x protease inhibitor cocktail (Roche) during sonication in a water bath. The sonication and clarification steps were performed as described in the preceding section. The resultant supernatants were transferred to fresh tubes, while the residual pellets were subjected to an additional solubilization process using 1M urea and 0.2% ProteaseMAX in 100 mM Tris-HCl during sonication in a water bath. Protein concentrations in the combined supernatants were determined using a BCA assay (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Protein aliquots (25 µg per sample) were then reduced by 5 mM dithiothreitol (Sigma) and alkylated by 15 mM iodoacetamide. The reaction was quenched by further addition of dithiothreitol and the peptides were proteolytically digested by trypsin (Promega). The resulting peptides were purified using a C18 Hypersep plate (Thermo Fisher Scientific), dried and labelled with TMTpro reagent. All samples were then pooled into a single vial, fractionated (as described below), and submitted for LC-MS/MS analysis. TMT-labelled tryptic peptides were dissolved in 20 mM ammonium hydroxide and approximately 130 µg of protein fractionated using a high-pH reversed-phase. Samples were loaded onto an Acquity bridged ethyl hybrid C18 UPLC column (Waters), and profiled with a linear gradient of 5–60% 20 mM ammonium hydroxide in ACN (pH 10.0). The chromatographic performance was monitored by sampling eluate with a UV detector (Ultimate 3000 UPLC, Thermo Scientific). Fractions were collected at 30 s intervals and combined in 12 samples concatenating 8-8 fractions representing the peak peptide elution.  Fractioned peptides were reconstituted in solvent A (2% ACN, 0.1% FA) and approximately 2 µg of samples were injected on a 50 cm long EASY-Spray C18 column (Thermo Fisher Scientific) connected to an Ultimate 3000 nanoUPLC system (Thermo Fisher Scientific). We used the following solvent B gradients: 4‑26% solvent B (98% ACN, 0.1% FA) over 90 min, 26-95% over 5 min, and 95% of solvent B for 5 min at a flow rate of 300 nL/min. Mass spectra were acquired on a Q Exactive HF hybrid quadrupole Orbitrap mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) ranging from 375 to 1700 m/z at a resolution of R=120,000 (at 200 m/z) targeting 5x106 ions for a maximum injection time of 100 ms. This was followed by data-dependent higher-energy collisional dissociation (HCD) fragmentation of precursor ions with a charge state 2+ to 7+, using 45 s dynamic exclusion. The tandem mass spectra of the top 18 precursor ions were acquired with a resolution of R=60,000, targeting 5x105 ions for a maximum injection time of 54 ms, setting quadrupole isolation width to 1.4 Th and normalized collision energy to 33%.
dataProcessingProtocol: Acquired raw data files were analyzed using Proteome Discoverer v2.5 (Thermo Fisher Scientific) with Sequest HT search engine against the human protein database (SwissProt). A maximum of two missed cleavage sites were allowed for full tryptic digestion, while setting the precursor and the fragment ion mass tolerance to 10 ppm and 0.02 Da, respectively. Carbamidomethylation of cysteine was specified as a fixed modification, while TMTpro on lysine and N-termini, oxidation on methionine, as well as deamidation of asparagine and glutamine, were set as dynamic modifications. Initial search results were filtered with 5% FDR using the Percolator node in Proteome Discoverer. Quantification was based on the TMT‑reporter ion abundances. The obtained lists of proteins and their abundances for each sample were then used to analyze the data in RStudio (version 1.4.1106).  Only proteins with at least 2 unique peptides detected were used for analysis. The abundances across samples were subjected to median normalization to correct potential systemic biases. For each protein, the significance of observed differential abundances between DIORA1 knockdown and non-targeting control groups was determined by performing a two‑tailed t-test and a Benjamini Hochberg correction. Fold changes were calculated by dividing the average protein abundance intensities of the DIORA1 knockdown samples by those of the non-targeting control samples for each protein. To obtain biological insight, gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA), using the HALLMARK gene sets, was conducted. Additional visualizations were generated using the pheatmap, ggplot2, bubbleHeatmap and limma R packages and GraphPad Prism 8. For evaluating the phosphoproteomic differences between conditions, phosphoproteomic abundances were first coupled and normalized to the corresponding total proteomic abundances (Aphospho/Atotal), as the input material was derived from the same cell sample for both analyses. The adjusted phosphoproteomic values were then normalized and processed as described above.
